elements.quote: Methods and Findings: All English-language published studies identified in our systematic search (up to February 3, 2021) examining the use of MSC-derived products to treat patients with COVID-19 were identified.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes a systematic search of studies to identify clinical studies of MSC-derived products for COVID-19, indicating the report is a systematic review.
The abstract does not provide an explicit statement of the main objective or a clearly framed review question.

elements.quote: All English-language published studies identified in our systematic search (up to February 3, 2021) examining the use of MSC-derived products to treat patients with COVID-19 were identified.
elements.reason: The abstract states the population/intervention inclusion (English-language clinical studies of MSC-derived products to treat COVID-19), but does not explicitly state detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: All English-language published studies identified in our systematic search (up to February 3, 2021)...
elements.reason: The abstract gives the date when the search was current (up to February 3, 2021) but does not list the information sources/databases within the abstract.

elements.quote: Risk of bias (RoB) was assessed for all studies.
elements.reason: The abstract states that risk of bias was assessed for all studies but does not specify the methods/tools used to assess risk of bias in the abstract.

elements.quote: Three of the controlled studies reported on mortality (primary analysis) and were pooled through random-effects meta-analysis. MSCs decreased the risk of death at study endpoint compared with controls (risk ratio, 0.18; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.04 to 0.74; P = .02; I2 = 0%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports that meta-analysis was performed and gives pooled effect estimates, indicating synthesis took place, but it does not fully describe the methods used to present and synthesize results in detail.

elements.quote: Nine studies were identified (189 patients), four of which were controlled (93 patients).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and summarizes key study grouping information (number of controlled studies and participants).

elements.quote: Three of the controlled studies reported on mortality (primary analysis) and were pooled through random-effects meta-analysis. MSCs decreased the risk of death at study endpoint compared with controls (risk ratio, 0.18; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.04 to 0.74; P = .02; I2 = 0%), although follow-up differed. Among secondary outcomes, interleukin-6 levels were most commonly reported and were decreased compared with controls (standardized mean difference, � 0.69; 95% CI, � 1.15 to � 0.22; P = .004; I2 = 0%) (n = 3 studies).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes, including the number of studies contributing to those outcomes and numerical effect estimates.

elements.quote: MSCs decreased the risk of death at study endpoint compared with controls (risk ratio, 0.18; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.04 to 0.74; P = .02; I2 = 0%).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports the summary estimate (risk ratio) with its 95% confidence interval.

elements.quote: MSCs decreased the risk of death at study endpoint compared with controls...
elements.reason: When comparing groups, the abstract indicates the direction of effect (decreased risk of death) and that MSCs are favored over controls.

elements.quote: Use of MSCs to treat COVID-19 appears promising; however, few studies were identified, and potential risk of bias was detected in all studies.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes important limitations, noting the small number of studies and the presence of potential risk of bias across studies.

elements.quote: Conclusion: Use of MSCs to treat COVID-19 appears promising; however, few studies were identified, and potential risk of bias was detected in all studies. More controlled studies that report uniform clinical outcomes and use MSC products that meet standard ISCT criteria should be performed.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and outlines implications for future research and practice.
The abstract does not report the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the registry name or registration number; registry information in the manuscript methods is present but not given in the abstract.

elements.quote: Our systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that MSCs are a promising treatment for COVID-19, although the certainty of this effect is limited by the small number of studies and modest numbers of patients enrolled, as well as substantial heterogeneity between studies in terms of study design, characterization of MSC products and outcome reporting.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge (MSCs look promising) and important uncertainties/limitations (small number of studies, modest patient numbers, substantial heterogeneity, inconsistent outcome reporting).

elements.quote: Background: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) and their secreted products are a promising therapy for COVID-19 given their immunomodulatory and tissue repair capabilities. Many small studies were launched at the onset of the pandemic, and repeated meta-analysis is critical to obtain timely and suf fi cient statistical power to determine ef fi cacy.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly explains the need for the review: many small studies exist and repeated meta-analysis is needed to gain sufficient power and timely evidence.

elements.quote: Although this initial number of published studies identi fi ed in our search is relatively small, many registered clinical trials dealing with the use of MSC-based products as a therapeutic intervention for COVID-19 were identi fi ed in a scoping review performed by our group [31].
elements.reason: The authors cite a prior scoping review by their group, indicating related prior work, but they do not explicitly discuss existing similar systematic reviews or explain how the current review updates or differs from prior systematic reviews; thus partial evidence for this item.

elements.quote: IL-6 levels have received signi fi cant attention as a mediator of damaging in fl ammation in COVID-19... Our analysis identi fi ed that MSCs lowered IL-6 levels. ... MSCs and their secreted factors may also support the regeneration of tissues damaged by the cytokine storm through release of growth factors including hepatocyte growth factor, keratinocyte growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor [56,57]. Thus, the pleiotropic anti-in fl ammatory and regenerative effects of MSCs may point to several potential mechanisms by which MSCs exert their apparent bene fi cial effect.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes proposed mechanisms of action for MSCs (immunomodulation, lowering IL-6, secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, regenerative effects).

No evidence was found of a logic model or diagram showing hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes; tables and text describe mechanisms but do not present a logic model.

elements.quote: Background: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) and their secreted products are a promising therapy for COVID-19 given their immunomodulatory and tissue repair capabilities. Many small studies were launched at the onset of the pandemic, and repeated meta-analysis is critical to obtain timely and suf fi cient statistical power to determine ef fi cacy.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the overall aim to evaluate MSCs/secreted products as a therapy for COVID-19 and the need for repeated meta-analysis to determine efficacy, which conveys the review's objective. However, it does not explicitly state detailed review questions or use a question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO) to frame the objectives.

Although the review concerns an intervention (MSCs/secretome), the evidence does not provide planned comparisons framed using PICO or a variant; no explicit statement of comparator, population details, outcomes, or specific intervention comparisons was found in the retrieved text.

elements.quote: All English-language, full-text, clinical studies examining the use of MSCs or their secretome (MSC-EVs, MSC-CM) as a therapeutic intervention for COVID-19 were included. Studies could be single armed (uncontrolled) or have a comparator or control groups (controlled). For the controlled studies, all randomization methods were considered acceptable (randomized, pseudo-randomized, and nonrandomized). Studies published in languages other than English, review articles, commentaries, editorials, letters, case reports, conference abstracts, unpublished gray literature and other study types (in vitro studies, preclinical animal studies, etc. ) were excluded. All symptomatic or asymptomatic patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (quantitative RT-PCR, antibody assay, etc. ) were included. MSCs derived from any known applicable tissue source (bone marrow, adipose tissue, umbilical cord, dental pulp, placenta, etc. ) were acceptable. MSCs could be obtained from syngeneic, allogeneic or xenogeneic tissues. All routes of MSC/secretome administration were acceptable (intravenous injection, aerosol inhalation, intramuscular injection, etc. ). MSC-based products could also be administered along with other therapeutic agents (antivirals, anti-cytokine drugs, immunomodulatory agents, etc. ). Studies exclusively investigating other non-MSC-based therapeutics were excluded.
elements.reason: The eligibility section specifies study designs, language, excluded study types, patient inclusion criteria, acceptable MSC sources, routes of administration, and inclusion of single-arm and controlled studies, covering study characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: All English-language, full-text, clinical studies ... were included. ... Studies published in languages other than English, review articles, commentaries, editorials, letters, case reports, conference abstracts, unpublished gray literature and other study types ... were excluded.
elements.reason: Report characteristics (language: English-only; publication/report status: full-text only, excluding conference abstracts and unpublished gray literature) are explicitly stated.
No text explicitly distinguishes exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported; retrieved evidence does not address this distinction.

elements.quote: For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) were calculated to determine the risk of death between the control and experimental groups at study endpoint. For continuous outcomes, the standardized mean difference (SMD) between control and experimental groups was calculated using random effects meta-analyses. ... Meta-analysis was performed only when three or more controlled studies reported on the same outcome.
elements.reason: The methods define groups used in syntheses (control vs experimental) and link these to the comparisons used for pooled analyses and criteria for conducting meta-analysis.

Although some restrictions are listed (e.g., English-language, full-text, exclusion of certain article types), no rationale explaining why these notable restrictions were applied is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: A systematic search of all clinical studies ... was conducted from 1947 to February 3, 2021, in Embase Classic+Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EBM Reviews and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the date range and the last search date (February 3, 2021) for the searches.

elements.quote: …was conducted from 1947 to February 3, 2021, in Embase Classic+Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EBM Reviews and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials.
elements.reason: Database names are provided and Ovid is specified for MEDLINE and EBM Reviews, but the search interface/platform is not fully specified for all databases (e.g., Embase platform not explicit) and coverage dates are given only as an overall range rather than database-specific coverage periods.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories are named nor are any date restrictions for such sources reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: All citations identified in the search were imported into Rayyan (https:// rayyan.qcri.org/) for management of search records.
elements.reason: Rayyan (with URL) is reported as a management tool, but no websites, search engines, or other online sources used to identify studies (with names and URLs) are reported as searched; thus the required details for searched websites/URLs are missing.
There is no report of contacting organisations or manufacturers to identify studies in the provided evidence.
The types of individuals (e.g., experts, authors) contacted to identify studies are not described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews captured by the search were also examined by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) to ensure that all relevant articles were captured.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies that reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were examined, which describes the types of reference lists examined.

elements.quote: The reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews captured by the search were also examined by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) to ensure that all relevant articles were captured.
elements.reason: Backward citation searching (examining reference lists) is reported, but seed reports, the citation index or platform used for forward/backward citation tracking, and the search date for citation searching are not specified.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted are named, and no dates covered or search methods for such sources are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The full search strategy is outlined in Figure S2.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the full search strategy is provided (outlined) in Figure S2, indicating the complete strategy was reported in the supplementary materials.

elements.quote: A systematic search of all clinical studies ... was conducted from 1947 to February 3, 2021, in Embase Classic+Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EBM Reviews and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials.
elements.reason: The date range and databases (search limits) are described, but no justification by reference to the eligibility criteria is provided in the supplied evidence.
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of adaptations is present in the provided evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms in the provided evidence.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence does not describe any validation of the search strategy (validation process or studies).

elements.quote: The search strategy was developed in collaboration with a health sciences librarian (R. Shorr) specializing in systematic review searches and was peer-reviewed by a second librarian according to the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) framework [34].
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the search strategy was peer-reviewed and names the PRESS framework, satisfying this reporting item.
No information is provided about the final conceptual structure when the search was not based on PICO, so this conditional item is not addressed in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: After duplicates were removed, the study titles and abstracts were screened in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan). After all potentially relevant titles and abstracts were identified, the full texts of all potentially relevant studies were reviewed in duplicate to determine final eligibility.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of reviewers (two) screening titles/abstracts and full texts, and names the reviewers.

elements.quote: the study titles and abstracts were screened in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan). ... the full texts of all potentially relevant studies were reviewed in duplicate to determine final eligibility.
elements.reason: It explicitly states reviewers worked independently (two independent reviewers) at both screening stages.

elements.quote: In cases of disagreement between the two reviewers, consensus was achieved through discussion with a third senior team member (D.S. Allan).
elements.reason: The process to resolve screening disagreements is described: discussion with a third senior team member to reach consensus.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes to obtain/confirm eligibility information from investigators.

elements.quote: Studies published in languages other than English, review articles, commentaries, editorials, letters, case reports, conference abstracts, unpublished gray literature and other study types ... were excluded.
elements.reason: The review excluded non-English full-text studies, so methods for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment do not apply.

elements.quote: All citations identified in the search were imported into Rayyan (https://rayyan.qcri.org/) for management of search records.
elements.reason: An automation/record-management tool (Rayyan) was used and its integration into the selection process is described.
No information is provided about externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed prior to screening.
No information is provided about internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use.
No details are provided on machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
No information is provided about use of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection.
No description is given of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived.

elements.quote: All relevant data was extracted in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) from the included studies using a standardized data extraction template in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft, Seattle, WA).
elements.reason: States explicitly that data extraction was performed in duplicate by two named reviewers, reporting the number of reviewers per report.

elements.quote: All relevant data was extracted in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) from the included studies using a standardized data extraction template in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft, Seattle, WA).
elements.reason: Specifies that the two data collectors worked independently ('two independent reviewers').

elements.quote: In cases of disagreement between the two reviewers, the differences were resolved through consultation with a senior team member (D.S. Allan).
elements.reason: Describes the process used to resolve disagreements: consultation with a senior team member.
No information is provided about processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators in the supplied evidence.
No description of automation tools used for data collection (including use, training, or validation) is reported in the supplied evidence.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported in the provided text.

elements.quote: ImageJ software was used to extract data in graphical format (https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/ download.html).
elements.reason: Specifies the software (ImageJ) used to extract data from figures.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies across reports are described in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Speci fi c data extracted from studies included study characteristics ( e.g. , authors, publication year, country of study), study design (characteristics of control group, sample size, length of observation period, planned preconditioning or alterations to MSCs or secreted factors before therapeutic use, MSC/secretome isolation and characterization methods, etc. ), patient characteristics (age, sex, comorbidities, COVID-19 severity, symptoms upon hospital admission, etc. ), intervention characteristics (MSC tissue source, MSC/secretome dose, route of administration, number of doses, whether MSC-based products met all of the minimal criteria established in guidelines by the International Society for Cellular Therapy [ISCT] [35] and/or Minimal Information for Studies of Extracellular Vesicles [MISEV] [36] criteria), all data pertaining to primary and secondary outcomes, and details concerning risk of bias (RoB) determination.
elements.reason: The methods list that data were extracted for primary and secondary outcomes and gives examples of outcome-related items (e.g., mortality and cytokine levels are discussed elsewhere), but it does not provide a comprehensive, defined list of all outcome domains sought nor formal definitions for each outcome domain.

No methods text specifies the time frame of measurement for each outcome domain; only isolated outcome time reporting (e.g., time to clinical improvement in results) appears, but no prespecified time frames for each outcome are described in the provided methods evidence.

The manuscript does not state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought; no explicit statement about seeking all compatible results is present in the provided methods excerpts.

Because the authors did not state whether all compatible results were sought, there is also no description of a process used to select among multiple compatible results; no selection process is reported in the provided evidence.

No evidence of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or their importance is reported in the provided materials; thus reporting such changes is not applicable based on the supplied evidence.

No evidence of changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains is reported in the provided materials; therefore this conditional item is not applicable based on the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Our primary analysis was mortality, given its clear relevance to lessening the paralytic and global impact of the pandemic.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly identify mortality as the outcome considered most important for interpretation (primary analysis) and provide a rationale for its prioritisation.

elements.quote: Speci fi c data extracted from studies included study characteristics ( e.g. , authors, publication year, country of study), study design (characteristics of control group, sample size, length of observation period, planned preconditioning or alterations to MSCs or secreted factors before therapeutic use, MSC/secretome isolation and characterization methods, etc. ), patient characteristics (age, sex, comorbidities, COVID-19 severity, symptoms upon hospital admission, etc. ), intervention characteristics (MSC tissue source, MSC/secretome dose, route of administration, number of doses, whether MSC-based products met all of the minimal criteria established in guidelines by the International Society for Cellular Therapy [ISCT] [35] and/or Minimal Information for Studies of Extracellular Vesicles [MISEV] [36] criteria), all data pertaining to primary and secondary outcomes, and details concerning risk of bias (RoB) determination.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines numerous non-outcome variables sought (study, study design, patient, intervention characteristics, outcomes, and RoB details).
No explicit description is provided of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: All relevant data was extracted in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) from the included studies using a standardized data extraction template in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft, Seattle, WA). ... RoB assessment was conducted using the Risk-of-Bias Tool for Randomized Trials (ROB 2) [37] for randomized controlled trials, the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS I tool) [38] for non-randomized controlled studies, and the Evidence Based Medicine (EBM) tool [39] for case series.
elements.reason: The authors report using a standardized data extraction template (Excel) and cite risk-of-bias tools; however, they do not explicitly cite or describe a specific published tool or guidance that determined which data items to collect (beyond their template and protocol registration reference), so the evidence partially supports this requirement.

elements.quote: RoB assessment was conducted using the Risk-of-Bias Tool for Randomized Trials (ROB 2) [37] for randomized controlled trials, the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS I tool) [38] for non-randomized controlled studies, and the Evidence Based Medicine (EBM) tool [39] for case series.
elements.reason: The manuscript names the risk-of-bias tools used (ROB 2, ROBINS-I, EBM tool) but does not specify tool versions or version numbers, so the requirement to specify tools and versions is only partially met.
No text in the provided evidence specifies the domains, components, or individual items assessed by any of the named risk-of-bias tools.

elements.quote: Regarding mortality, one RCT [43] was found to have low risk of bias, and the other RCT [41] had a risk of bias of "some concerns"(Table S1)... For nonrandomized studies [40,42], both were found to have a moderate risk of bias (Table S3). Of the included case series, three were found to be of good quality [45,47,48] and two of fair quality [44,46] (Table S4).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports overall risk-of-bias judgments for included studies (e.g., 'low', 'some concerns', 'moderate', 'good', 'fair'), but it does not describe the explicit rules or criteria used to derive those overall judgements from domain-level assessments.
No adaptations to existing risk-of-bias tools are described in the provided evidence.
The manuscript reports use of established tools (ROB 2, ROBINS-I, EBM tool); there is no indication that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created, so this item does not apply.

elements.quote: All relevant data was extracted in duplicate by two independent reviewers (A.M. Kirkham, M. Monaghan) ... In cases of disagreement between the two reviewers, the differences were resolved through consultation with a senior team member (D.S. Allan). ... and details concerning risk of bias (RoB) determination.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that data were extracted in duplicate by two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by a senior team member, and it mentions RoB determination in the same context; however, it does not explicitly state how many reviewers specifically assessed risk of bias, whether those RoB assessments were done independently, nor detailed disagreement-resolution procedures specific to RoB assessment.
No processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators (e.g., contacting authors) are described in the provided evidence.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) were calculated to determine the risk of death between the control and experimental groups at study endpoint. For continuous outcomes, the standardized mean difference (SMD) between control and experimental groups was calculated using random effects meta-analyses. ... All data is presented with 95% con fi dence intervals (CIs).
elements.reason: The methods section explicitly specifies effect measures for dichotomous (risk ratios) and continuous (standardized mean difference) outcomes and states 95% CIs are reported.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size (e.g., small/medium/large SMD cutoffs) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
No methods for re-expressing synthesized results using an alternative effect measure (e.g., converting SMD to odds ratio) are described in the provided evidence.
The authors state which effect measures were used but do not provide a justification or rationale for the choice of those effect measures in the provided text.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was performed only when three or more controlled studies reported on the same outcome. Outcomes that were reported in fewer than three controlled studies or for which adequate data for inclusion in meta-analysis was not provided were analyzed in a descriptive manner.
elements.reason: The authors describe a clear, pre-specified decision rule for which studies would be included in quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis) versus descriptive synthesis (i.e., requiring ≥3 controlled studies reporting the same outcome), which is a process used to decide eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote:
The results from individual studies were pooled for meta-analysis using Review Manager (version 5.4) Systematic Review Software (https://training.cochrane.org/online-learning/core-software- cochrane-reviews/revman/revman-5-download). For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) were calculated to determine the risk of death between the control and experimental groups at study endpoint. For continuous outcomes, the standardized mean difference (SMD) between control and experimental groups was calculated using random effects meta-analyses. Meta-analysis was performed only when three or more controlled studies reported on the same outcome. Outcomes that were reported in fewer than three controlled studies or for which adequate data for inclusion in meta-analysis was not provided were analyzed in a descriptive manner. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic.

ImageJ software was used to extract data in graphical format (https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/ download.html).
